No validated tool in this toolkit checks the attainable-value set of a median or quartile of integer data at n=12/n=15, so the quartile granularity (values printed as .3/.8/.5) was deliberately NOT hand-derived. The primary cognitive outcome is therefore heavily right-censored: in several early-training columns the large majority of animals never found the platform and were assigned the ceiling. The paper nonetheless plots these as mean ± SEM (Figs 7 and 8) and analyses them with Kruskal-Wallis. A mean computed over a censored variable understates the true latency by an amount that depends on how many animals hit the cap, which differs by group and by day, so between-group mean differences in the early days are confounded with differential censoring. Kruskal-Wallis is at least rank-based and so partially robust, but the plotted means and SEMs - which are what a reader interprets - are not. Counts are read from the tool's occurrence tally; I did not independently recount them, and the exact per-column denominators were not verified because the 2.6 MB grid could not be read without sampling.

findings.title: Multiplicity not computable
findings.description: The multiplicity arithmetic returned n_tests = 0: all 14 comparisons were dropped rather than coerced, because every p is printed as a bound rather than a value. So no family-wise or false-discovery correction can be computed for this paper at all, and no surviving-claims interval can be quoted. To be fair to the authors, this is NOT a case of uncorrected testing: Dunn's post-hoc (used for the nonparametric families) and the stated Bonferroni correction (used for the ANOVA families) both do control multiplicity. The finding is that the reporting makes the correction impossible to verify, not that it is absent.
